blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A readiness probe thread runs `while (!warm) { probes++; }`, where `warm` is a plain boolean field that the startup thread sets to true about 2 seconds after launch. On the staging host the probe thread is still in that loop an hour later, long after `warm` was set. What explains it?

options.text: The JIT compiled the loop to read `warm` once before it starts, since nothing orders the startup thread's write before the probe thread's reads
options.says: without a happens-before edge the JIT may read a plain field once and loop on that value; volatile forbids it

options.text: The JIT compiled the loop to read `warm` once before it starts, since a compiled loop keeps every field it reads in a register for good
options.says: compiled code reads a volatile field on every pass; the freedom to hoist exists only because the field is plain and nothing synchronizes

options.text: The loop reads `warm` on every pass, but from the probe core's cache, which keeps the old value until that cache line is evicted
options.says: the hardware keeps caches coherent, and the interpreted loop sees the write; caches are not what hides it

options.text: The loop reads `warm` on every pass, but from a copy of the field that the probe thread took when it started
options.says: the interpreted loop sees the write, so nothing was copied at thread start; the compiled loop stopped reading the field

origin.section: Without volatile, a Reader May Never See the Write: the JIT May Read a Plain Field Once

questions.stem: A settings loader runs `Settings s = new Settings(); current = s; s.timeoutMs = 2500;`, where `current` is a volatile field and `timeoutMs` is a plain int field of `Settings`. A request thread reads `current.timeoutMs` after the assignment to `current`. Which values can the request see?

options.text: Only 2500, since the write to `timeoutMs` and the volatile write to `current` are made by the same thread, and a volatile write publishes all of its thread's writes
options.says: a volatile write publishes only the writes its thread made before it; this one came after

options.text: Only 2500, since the write to `timeoutMs` goes through `s`, the object `current` refers to, so it is published together with `current`
options.says: volatile covers the field, not the object it points to; timeoutMs stays a plain field

options.text: 0 or 2500, since the write to `timeoutMs` comes after the volatile write to `current`, and no later volatile write publishes it to the request
options.says: only writes made before the volatile write ride on it; the request may see the default, and no later read is promised to see 2500

options.text: 0 or 2500, since the write to `timeoutMs` is published only when the loader's method returns, and it may not have returned yet
options.says: returning from a method publishes nothing; the reason is that the write came after the volatile write

origin.section: A Volatile Write Publishes What Was Written Before It, Not What Comes After

questions.stem: A firewall keeps `volatile List<String> blocked = new ArrayList<>()`. An admin thread blocks an address with `blocked.add("203.0.113.7")`, and request threads call `blocked.contains(ip)`. What does `volatile` contribute here?

options.text: Each `add` reaches the request threads, since every request reads the volatile field `blocked` before it reads the list
options.says: reading the volatile reference publishes only writes made before a volatile write to it; add writes inside the list and never writes the field

options.text: Each `add` reaches the request threads, since `add` is one method call on a volatile reference and so it is one atomic write
options.says: an add is several plain writes inside the ArrayList; volatile makes only reads and writes of the field itself atomic

options.text: Nothing for the `add` calls, since the field is written once, when it is assigned, and every `add` writes inside the list instead
options.says: volatile covers the field, not the object it points to; publishing a change would take a new list assigned to the field

options.text: Nothing for the `add` calls, since `volatile` orders writes to primitive fields only, and `blocked` holds a reference
options.says: a volatile reference field is published like any other volatile field; the problem is that add never writes it

origin.section: volatile Covers One Field: Values That Must Agree Are Swapped as One Immutable Object

questions.stem: A status page reads `lastBeat`, a `long` of epoch milliseconds written every second by a heartbeat thread. The field is plain, and the service also runs on a 32-bit JVM. Apart from staleness, what can the status page read there?

options.text: It can read a value no thread wrote, since the JLS lets a plain 64-bit write be carried out as two separate 32-bit writes
options.says: plain accesses are bitwise atomic only up to 32 bits and for references; volatile long makes each read and write atomic

options.text: It can read a value no thread wrote, since the JLS lets a 32-bit JVM store only the low 32 bits of a plain `long` field
options.says: both halves are stored; a plain long may be written as two halves, and the reader can fall between them

options.text: It reads only values the heartbeat wrote, since the JLS requires a plain field of a primitive type to be written in one step
options.says: the JLS (17.7) and VarHandle's javadoc allow a plain long or double write to be split; only volatile ones are promised atomic

options.text: It reads only values the heartbeat wrote, since the JLS lets a write be split only when two threads write the same field
options.says: one writer is enough: the reader can fall between the two halves of that writer's write

origin.section: volatile Makes Each Read and Each Write Atomic, Never a Read Followed by a Write

concepts: A plain long or double may be read and written as two 32-bit halves; a volatile one is read and written whole.
Without volatile or another happens-before edge, the JIT may read a plain field once, so a loop on a flag set by another thread may never end; volatile makes every read see the latest write.
A volatile write publishes the writes its thread made before it; writes made after it, such as filling an object already assigned to the field, are not published.
A volatile reference does not make the object or array it points to volatile; writes inside it are plain writes.
